Shelby County v. Holder. In 2013, the Supreme Court gutted a crucial protection of the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Shelby County, Alabama, a jurisdiction with a long history of racial discrimination, challenged the constitutionality of Section 5, which required that jurisdictions with a history of discrimination obtain federal preclearance before changing voting rules.

Chief Justice John Roberts wrote for a 5 to 4 majority. He argued that conditions had changed sufficiently that the pre-clearance regime was no longer justified under the 15th Amendment. The decision did not overturn Section 5 entirely, but it invalidated the formula Congress used to identify which jurisdictions required federal approval. This effectively halted the preclearance process.

Within months of the decision, states previously covered by the preclearance requirement began enacting restrictive voting laws. They passed strict voter ID laws, reduced early voting periods, purged voter rolls, and closed polling places in minority districts. Voting rights advocates argue the decision unleashed voter suppression. Defenders contend the Voting Rights Act had succeeded and become outdated. Whatever the debate, the practical effect was immediate.

Shelby County remains one of the most consequential civil rights decisions in decades. It reshaped American voting rights and electoral politics. The decision represents the conservative counter-reaction to the civil rights victories of an earlier era, even as a new generation of voting restrictions emerged to replace the ones courts had struck down.
